Metric note: Measures the relative advantage or disadvantage of households based on income, occupation, education, housing, and related characteristics. Higher scores indicate greater advantage, and lower scores indicate greater disadvantage.  The index is standardised with a mean of 1000 and a standard deviation of 100.

"Measures how culturally diverse a suburb is based on the distribution of ancestries. CDI close to 1 means very culturally diverse (no single ancestry dominates). CDI close to 0 means homogeneous population (one ancestry dominates). A rising CDI over time can signal a transitioning suburb
Ranking: potentially early in its property growth cycle. Metric varies from 0 to 1.

Source: Indicates how international the suburb’s population background is, by measuring % of residents have at least one parent born overseas. Metric varies from 0 to 100%. Can be a proxy for migration-driven demand and social change

Measures the overall education level of residents by measuring % of residents that have completed high-school. Highly educated suburbs tend to have higher incomes, attract better amenities, and experience steadier property growth. Metric varies from 0 to 100%.
Measures the % of public or community housing in the suburb. Very high percentages can suggest socio-economic disadvantage. Metric varies from 0 to 100%.
"Indicates the proportion of dwellings that are owned outright or with a mortgage. Higher ownership rates are usually associated with greater stability
KPI calculation: and stronger local investment. Metric varies from 0 to 100%.

Source: "Proportion of dwellings renting below a threshold ($450 per week). Indicates affordability — lower value suburbs are more affordable and will be of interest to renters. Metric varies from 0 to 100%.
"Measures how long residents tend to stay in the suburb
KPI Name: as measured by % of residents who stayed in the same community for 5 years or more. Higher values mean lower turnover and more stable
KPI calculation: tight knit communities. Metric varies from 0 to 100%.

Metric note: Measures the potential for households to move within the area. High values indicate higher turnover and dynamic population changes. Metric varies from 0 to 100%.
Indicates the proportion of households identified as young families. Metric varies from 0 to 100%.
The proportion of households falling in the most disadvantaged SEIFA quartile (Q1), identifying suburbs with the highest concentration of socio-economic vulnerability
The proportion of residents aged 65 and over, identifying suburbs with strong demand for low-maintenance housing, aged-care services and downsizer developments.
The proportion of dwellings that are flats, apartments, townhouses or semi-detached, identifying suburbs oriented toward medium- and high-density housing stock
The proportion of rented dwellings with weekly rent of $650 or above, identifying suburbs with strong premium rental yield potential

Combines Prosperity, Learning Level, Rental Access and Social Housing into one investment score. Gives investors one easy score instead of analysing four KPIs separately. This is the first composite KPI. Investment Potential Score=(Prosperity Score*25%)+(Learning Level*35%)+(Rental Access*25%)+(Social Housing*15%)

The share of a suburb's population who are third-generation-plus Australian - born in Australia, with both parents also born in Australia. A high score points to a long-settled, low-turnover family community.

Field Name: Final score = Sum of all indices
